candidates.attacker_control: The testPlanUrl value: in freestyle jobs it is the stored field editable by anyone with Item/Configure on that job (the existing Secret field is resubmitted as its encrypted value, so the attacker does not need to know the API key to have it decrypted and forwarded); in pipelines it is whatever the Jenkinsfile / parameters feed into zohoQEngineTestPlanExecution(testPlanUrl: ...). The attacker also controls portalName path segment content (any string without '/') and the build name.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the request is not merely a form-validation call: doCheckTestPlanUrl (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:63-75) performs no network I/O, so the SSRF/credential flow requires a build, not just an HTTP GET. Checked redirect handling: the code does not set a redirect policy, and java.net.http.HttpClient defaults to NEVER, so credentials are not automatically re-sent to a redirect target. Checked header injection: Java HttpClient rejects CR/LF header values, and the two numeric IDs are validated as positive longs via extractLongValue, so no direct URL/path injection through those fields. Checked Hostname verification/TLS: default HttpClient trust is used, so this is not a TLS-bypass finding. Counterargument: the person who configures the job is normally trusted to enter the API key, and Jenkins treats Item/Configure users as able to use a job's credentials, which weakens the boundary; the finding therefore depends on the (common) case where the secret was entered by someone else and is not readable to the attacker.
candidates.impact: Disclosure/exfiltration of the stored Zoho QEngine API key (a Jenkins Secret) to an attacker-controlled host, and a controller-originated request primitive to arbitrary HTTPS hosts (limited SSRF: attacker chooses host and can inject a query/fragment from the unvalidated portalName; path is otherwise the fixed QEngine API prefix/suffix and the answer is only partially reflected through the printed JSON message/status fields). Stolen API keys allow acting against the victim's Zoho QEngine tenant.
candidates.prerequisites: A user able to write the builder's testPlanUrl for a job whose configuration contains a Secret API key, plus the ability to run/trigger the build. No admin rights and no knowledge of the API key are required for the capture step itself if the job's config is re-saved with a new URL while keeping the API-key field untouched. Outbound HTTPS from the controller must be reachable to the attacker host; if the configured host resolves internally, the same code path gives a controller-side SSRF.
candidates.root_cause: The plugin never constrains the host of the configured test plan URL. QEnginePluginBuilder.perform() accepts testPlanUrl when it merely starts with "https://" and splits into exactly six '/' segments, deriving requestUrl = protocolSplit[0] + "//" + resourceSplit[0] (the literal host) with no allowlist against Zoho/QEngine domains. CommonUtils.executeTestPlan()/getTestPlanStatus() then build the request URI by string concatenation and unconditionally attach "Authorization: Bearer " + apiKey.getPlainText() to that host. Only the two numeric IDs are validated (positive longs) and portalName is not validated at all; the host is never checked.
candidates.title: API key and server-side request sent to an unvalidated, user-controlled testPlanUrl host
candidates.trace: 1) Configured testPlanUrl e.g. https://attacker.example/portal/projects/1/testplans/2 -> split("//") = ["https:", "attacker.example/portal/projects/1/testplans/2"], split("/") = 6 segments -> requestUrl="https://attacker.example", portalName="portal", projectID="1", testPlanID="2" (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:114-122). 2) perform() calls CommonUtils.executeTestPlan(apiKey, requestUrl, ...) (lines 156-157). 3) executeUrl = requestUrl + "/api/v1/integration/..." (CommonUtils.java:52-53) and the request is built with Authorization: Bearer <plaintext Secret> on host attacker.example (lines 57-59). 4) The PATCH also carries the build name in JSON; getTestPlanStatus() repeats the same Authorization header on every poll to the same host (lines 127-130). 5) Response JSON fields ("message" on non-202, "scheduleexecution.status" on 202) are printed to the build console, giving the attacker a partial read-back from the server contacted.
candidates.unverified: No runtime exploitation attempted. Not verified in-repo whether the Jenkins version in use re-submits the stored encrypted Secret value unchanged through the form/DataBoundConstructor path (config.jelly is absent from this snapshot, so the UI binding could not be inspected), nor whether any deployment restricts testPlanUrl to admin-only. Not verified whether the Java HttpClient in the target JDK/Jenkins version sends URI userinfo or normalizes the path, and no external host or Zoho endpoint was contacted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery with CWE-522/credential exposure (insertion of sensitive information into a request to an externally controlled location)

coverage_summary: All 14 files reported by get_source_scope were enumerated and every file was read (the two Java sources in full: CommonUtils.java 1-262 and QEnginePluginBuilder.java 1-229; plus pom.xml, README, both workflows, dependabot.yml, .mvn/extensions.xml, .gitignore, LICENSE and the four help HTML files). Search was used for checkPermission, URL/Secret/getPlainText patterns. No source file was skipped by the safety filters (0 binary, 0 oversized, 0 sensitive-name, 0 symlink exclusions). The snapshot contains no test sources, no config.jelly/Jelly views, no build scripts and no other Java code; behavior was analyzed statically only, without compiling or executing anything.
limitations: Static, read-only review: no code was executed, no Jenkins instance was started, and no request was made to any host; the candidate remains an unconfirmed lead.

The snapshot is missing src/main/resources/.../QEnginePluginBuilder/config.jelly and any test sources, so Jelly data binding, secret re-submission semantics and intended admin-only usage of testPlanUrl could not be inspected.

Jenkins core/API behavior (HttpRequest.newBuilder rejecting relative URIs, no redirect following by default, Item/Configure trust model for job credentials) was reasoned from framework knowledge, not from the Jenkins sources in this snapshot.
The server-side impact at the Zoho QEngine end (what a stolen key authorizes) and the reachability of internal HTTPS endpoints from a typical controller were not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing permission check on the form-validation endpoints doCheckTestPlanUrl / doCheckApiKey / doCheckMaxWaitTime / doCheckBuildName (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:61-97, the first explicitly silenced with @SuppressWarnings("lgtm[jenkins/no-permission-check]"))
rejected_leads.reason: Real deviation from Jenkins hardening guidance (any user with Overall/Read can invoke them), but none of the four methods changes state or returns sensitive data: they only test emptiness, an https prefix plus six path segments, or a positive integer, and return a fixed ok/warning message. No attacker-reachable impact beyond a harmless format oracle, so it is a hardening opportunity rather than a vulnerability of the required evidence standard.

rejected_leads.lead: Integer overflow / unbounded sleep in getTestPlanStatus polling interval (CommonUtils.java:123-124: (maxWaitTime * 60) / (pollCount - 1) * 1000 in int arithmetic, only negative values defaulted at QEnginePluginBuilder.java:146-148)
rejected_leads.reason: A large or crafted maxWaitTime can overflow the interval to a negative/absurd value and abort or stall that one build, but only the configuring user's own job and its executor are affected; no cross-user or controller-wide denial of service was demonstrated in source.

rejected_leads.lead: Validation failures use listener.error(...) but execution continues (QEnginePluginBuilder.java:108-144), so executeTestPlan is still invoked with requestUrl == null
rejected_leads.reason: Explored as a possible request to an unexpected target: the concatenated string "null/api/v1/..." is a relative URI and HttpRequest.newBuilder requires an absolute URI, so the call throws and the build is marked FAILURE. No request is emitted, no impact.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded/inefficient response reading helper readContents (CommonUtils.java:217-243, 500k-char buffer) and broad 'catch (Exception)' swalling in getQEnginePluginVersion
rejected_leads.reason: readContents is dead code in this snapshot (no callers) and the exception swallowing only degrades diagnostics; neither is attacker-influenced in a concrete way.

rejected_leads.lead: GitHub Actions supply-chain exposure: .github/workflows/cd.yaml grants contents: write and passes MAVEN_USERNAME/MAVEN_TOKEN to jenkins-infra/github-reusable-workflows@v1 (a mutable tag); dependabot.yml updates pinned refs monthly
rejected_leads.reason: Mutable-tag pinning is a hardening concern, but the called workflow is the official jenkins-infra reusable release workflow triggered only via workflow_dispatch/check_run; no untrusted-input influence over the called workflow was identified in the snapshot.
Test-only scope, not packaged into the HPI, and no usage is present in the snapshot; not an exploitable repository vulnerability.

summary: Reviewed the full 14-file snapshot (all files listed by get_source_scope; the two Java sources read end-to-end). The plugin is a Jenkins build step that takes a user-supplied "Test Plan Execution URL", a Secret API key, a max wait time and a build name, then PATCH/POSTs to Zoho QEngine with the API key in an Authorization header. The only security-relevant sink in the whole tree is the server-side HTTP request in CommonUtils: the target host comes entirely from the configured testPlanUrl (validated only for an "https://" prefix and six slash-separated path segments; no host/domain allowlist), and the decrypted Secret API key is attached to that request. That is the single strongest source-evidenced lead: a user who can set/replace the URL (Item/Configure on the job, or build-parameter input wired into the step) can direct the Jenkins controller to connect to an arbitrary HTTPS endpoint and capture the job's stored plaintext API key, plus obtain a limited SSRF/read primitive via the parsed "message"/"status" fields echoed into the build log. No injection, deserialization, XSS or command-execution sink exists in the snapshot.
